newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FOCUS-Anglo enjoys rich Q4, sees tough 1997.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Anglo enjoys rich Q4, sees tough 1997.

text.p: The world's largest gold producer Anglo American Corp of South Africa Ltd on Thursday announced a nine percent profit increase for the three months ended December compared to the preceding quarter.
But the mining giant faces a tough 1997 with the gold price weak in both dollar and rand terms and says its mines will have to "get smart" to weather the current market situation.

"During this period of price weakness the five companies will concentrate on those aspects of their business that they can influence directly -- smart mining strategies, improved operational efficiencies, better labour productivity," said Bobby Godsell, Anglogold chief executive.

"This will help us weather present storms. It will also have us well placed to take advantage of the better times which will undoubtedly come," he told analysts and reporters at a presentation of the December quarter gold results.
Reaping the fruits of a weaker rand and steady bullion price in those three months, Anglo raised available profit for its five gold mines in the December quarter by nine percent to 348 million rand.
Gold output rose three percent to 54 tonnes and the average gold price received rose two percent to 55,756 rand ($12,120) per kg.
But the bullion price has recently been punished by investment funds and speculators, breaking below the key $350 per ounce support level on Wednesday. It was last bid at $349.60.
On top of that, the rand was looking steady and might see some slight firming in 1997 -- putting an end to the South African mines' rich gains from the rand gold price.
Anglo said its largest mine, Free State Consolidated Gold Mines Ltd, would see production fall 6.4 percent this year, to 78 tonnes.
Other mines in its stable should produce more and the overall target for gold production in 1997 was put at 212.5 tonnes, one tonne less than in 1996.
Vaal Exploration and Mining Co Ltd announced plans to implement a new working calendar which could add 25 more shifts to the mine's operational year.
Chief operating officer Dick Fisher said the new calendar should be implemented by the end of the second quarter of 1997, but would only win four extra shifts during the current financial year.
Anglo said it expected an eventual recovery in the bullion price based on robust physical demand for the metal.
"There will be a turning (point) when gold will come back into favour," said Anglogold marketing director Kelvin Williams.
"We really see the gold market as being balanced on a robust gold offtake (and) satisfactory demand," he said.
But this, he added, was notwithstanding the negative implications of market anxieties about sales of central bank gold which was a real issue but "not something that will go on into the 2000s".
Williams said initial indications were that physical demand for gold in 1996 had matched the record levels seen in 1995. ($=4.63 rand)
